questions.question: How do you set up a Mockito test class in JUnit 5?
questions.title: Mockito Test Setup JUnit 5 | Java Fresher Interview
questions.direct_answer: Add @ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class) to the class, declare @Mock for dependencies, and @InjectMocks for the class under test. MockitoExtension processes these annotations automatically before each test, no manual setup needed.

interviewer_intent.testing: Practical Mockito setup — can you write a test class from scratch?
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Forgetting @ExtendWith and wondering why @Mock is null
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show a complete test class skeleton with all annotations in context

sections.title: Setting Up a Mockito Test Class
sections.content: **Mockito** helps you create test doubles (mocks) for dependencies so you can unit test a class in isolation. In JUnit 5, you use **@ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class)** to tell JUnit to initialize Mockito's annotation processing before each test. Then you declare **@Mock** on fields representing dependencies (like repositories or services) and **@InjectMocks** on the class you're testing. MockitoExtension automatically creates mock instances and injects them into your test subject. This eliminates the manual `MockitoAnnotations.openMocks(this)` call you'd need otherwise. Think of it like Spring's dependency injection, but for test objects: you declare what you need, and the framework wires it together. The result is cleaner test code where you focus on behavior, not plumbing.

sections.title: Complete Mockito Test Class Example
Key Points
content: **@ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class)**: enables Mockito annotation processing in JUnit 5
**@Mock**: creates a mock instance of the declared type automatically before each test
**@InjectMocks**: creates the test subject and injects all @Mock fields into it
**MockitoExtension**: handles mock lifecycle (creation, injection, reset) so you don't manually call openMocks()
**Strict stubbing**: enabled by default in MockitoExtension — fails tests if stubs are unused or called with wrong arguments
**No manual initialization**: unlike JUnit 4, you don't need MockitoAnnotations.openMocks(this) in a @BeforeEach method
**Multiple mocks**: you can declare as many @Mock fields as needed — all are injected into @InjectMocks

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: To set up a Mockito test class in JUnit 5, you add the at-ExtendWith annotation with MockitoExtension dot class at the top of your test class. This tells JUnit to activate Mockito's annotation processing. Then you declare your dependencies as fields with the at-Mock annotation. For example, if you're testing an OrderService that depends on an OrderRepository and an EmailService, you'd declare those two as at-Mock fields. Finally, you declare the class under test with at-InjectMocks. Mockito automatically creates mock instances of the dependencies and injects them into your service before each test runs. You don't need to write any setup method or call openMocks manually. One thing to watch out for: if you forget the at-ExtendWith annotation, your at-Mock fields will be null and your tests will fail with NullPointerException. The extension is what activates the whole annotation scanning process. This setup is cleaner than JUnit 4 because you don't need a runner or a manual setup method — the extension handles everything. It also enables strict stubbing by default, which catches bugs like unused stubs that indicate your test isn't checking what you think it is.

questions.question: What is strict stubbing mode in Mockito and why is it useful?
questions.title: Mockito Strict Stubbing | Java Fresher Interview
questions.direct_answer: Strict stubbing fails tests if a stub is declared but never called, or called with different arguments. It prevents test pollution from outdated or incorrect stubs. MockitoExtension enables STRICT_STUBS by default in Mockito 2.23+.

interviewer_intent.testing: Depth of Mockito knowledge — shows you've used it seriously
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Getting errors from STRICT_STUBS and disabling it instead of fixing the unnecessary stub
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that STRICT_STUBS improves test quality by catching stale stubs that indicate test drift

sections.title: Understanding Strict Stubbing Mode
sections.content: **Strict stubbing** is Mockito's quality enforcement mode that detects unused or mismatched stubs in your tests. When you stub a method with `when(...).thenReturn(...)`, strict mode tracks whether that stub is actually invoked during the test. If you stub `repository.findById(1L)` but your code calls `findById(2L)`, or never calls it at all, Mockito fails the test with a **UnnecessaryStubbingException**. This is like a compiler warning for tests: it catches copy-paste errors, refactoring drift, and logic bugs where your test setup doesn't match what your code actually does. Before strict mode, these stale stubs would silently pass, giving false confidence. The analogy: it's like your IDE warning about unused imports — they're not breaking anything, but they indicate drift between intent and reality. MockitoExtension enables this by default, so you get the benefit automatically in JUnit 5.

sections.title: Strict Stubbing Catching a Bug
Key Points
content: **Strict stubbing**: detects unused stubs (declared but never invoked) and argument mismatches (stub for arg X, called with arg Y)
**UnnecessaryStubbingException**: thrown when a stub is defined but not used during test execution
**Enabled by default**: MockitoExtension in JUnit 5 enables STRICT_STUBS automatically since Mockito 2.23+
**Test quality**: catches refactoring bugs where stubs drift from actual code paths
**Lenient stubbing**: use @Mock(lenient=true) or lenient().when(...) to opt out for specific stubs when necessary
**Copy-paste detector**: helps identify tests copied from another test but not updated properly
**ArgumentMatchers**: strict mode also validates that matchers (any(), eq()) match actual call arguments

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: Strict stubbing is a quality mode in Mockito that fails your test if you declare a stub that's never actually used, or if the method is called with different arguments than you stubbed. Let's say you stub repository dot findById with ID one, but your code actually calls it with ID two. Without strict stubbing, the test would pass even though your stub is meaningless — the method returns null or a default mock, and you might not notice the bug. With strict stubbing enabled, Mockito throws an UnnecessaryStubbingException and tells you exactly which stub wasn't used. This is really useful because it catches copy-paste errors. You copy a test, change the test name, but forget to update the stub arguments. Strict mode catches that immediately. It's enabled by default when you use MockitoExtension in JUnit 5, so you get the benefit automatically. One mistake freshers make is seeing this error and thinking Mockito is broken, so they disable it with lenient mode. That's the wrong fix. The right fix is to update your stub to match what your code actually does, or remove the stub if it's not needed. Strict stubbing improves test quality by ensuring your setup matches your execution — it's like having a linter for your test doubles.

questions.question: How do you create a mock manually without annotations in Mockito?
questions.title: Mockito.mock() Manual Creation | Java Fresher Interview
questions.direct_answer: Use Mockito.mock(ClassName.class) to create a mock programmatically. This is equivalent to @Mock but done inline. Use it when you need to create a mock dynamically or outside a test class context — e.g., in a helper method or when the class is generic.

interviewer_intent.testing: Knowledge of both annotation and programmatic Mockito styles
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not knowing the manual form — only knowing @Mock annotation
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain when you'd choose manual creation over annotations: dynamic mocking, generic types, factory methods

sections.title: Creating Mocks Programmatically
sections.content: **Mockito.mock(Class.class)** is the programmatic way to create a mock at runtime, giving you full control over when and where the mock is created. Unlike **@Mock** which requires annotation scanning by MockitoExtension, the static method works anywhere in your code. You'd use it when you need to create mocks **dynamically** based on test input, when working with **generic types** that annotations can't express cleanly, or in **helper methods** that build test fixtures. Think of it like the difference between constructor injection (declarative, framework-managed) and new keyword (imperative, you control it). Both create the same type of mock object — they just differ in who controls the creation timing. The annotation style is preferred for standard test fields because it's cleaner and ties into MockitoExtension's lifecycle, but the programmatic style is your fallback when you need flexibility.

sections.title: Programmatic Mock Creation
Key Points
content: **Mockito.mock(Class.class)**: static method that creates a mock instance immediately — no annotations required
**No extension needed**: works without @ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class) because it's a plain method call
**Dynamic creation**: useful when you need to create mocks in loops, conditionally, or based on test parameters
**Generic types**: helps when mocking parameterized types like List<String> where annotations are clumsy
**Helper methods**: ideal for test utility methods that build complex fixture objects with multiple mocks
**Lifecycle control**: you control when the mock is created and can store it in local variables or fields as needed
**Same mock object**: produces identical mock behavior to @Mock — the difference is creation timing, not functionality

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: To create a mock manually without annotations, you call Mockito dot mock and pass the class type. For example, Mockito dot mock PaymentGateway dot class gives you a mock instance right there. This is functionally identical to declaring a field with at-Mock — both produce the same type of mock object. The difference is when and where it's created. With at-Mock, the MockitoExtension creates it before each test automatically. With the static method, you create it exactly when you call the method, giving you full control. You'd use the programmatic style in a few scenarios. First, when you need to create mocks dynamically, like in a loop or based on test input. Second, when you're working with generic types — mocking a List of String is cleaner with the static method than trying to express that in an annotation. Third, in helper methods that build test fixtures. If you have a factory method that assembles a complex object graph for multiple tests, you'd use Mockito dot mock inside that helper rather than trying to inject annotated fields. One pitfall: if you create a mock manually, you're responsible for its lifecycle. It won't be automatically reset between tests like at-Mock fields are. For standard test fields, prefer at-Mock because it's cleaner and integrates with strict stubbing. But when you need flexibility, the static method is your tool.

questions.question: How do you verify that a method was never called in Mockito?
questions.title: Mockito verify never() | Java Fresher Interview
questions.direct_answer: Use verify(mock, never()).method(args) to assert a method was NOT called. Also useful: verifyNoInteractions(mock) — asserts no methods were called on the mock. Use these to test negative scenarios like 'email should not be sent when order fails validation'.

interviewer_intent.testing: Negative testing with Mockito — important for verifying side effects don't happen
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not knowing how to verify a method wasn't called — only knowing verify() for positive cases
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Give a concrete scenario: when validation fails, the database save should NOT be called

sections.title: Verifying Methods Were Never Called
sections.content: **Negative verification** is how you assert that certain side effects did NOT happen in your test. Use **verify(mock, never()).method(args)** to confirm a specific method was not invoked, or **verifyNoInteractions(mock)** to assert nothing was called on the entire mock. This is crucial for testing error paths, validation failures, and conditional logic. For example, if an order fails validation, you want to verify that `emailService.sendConfirmation()` was never called — sending a confirmation email for an invalid order would be a bug. Think of it like testing the negative space in a painting: you're not just checking what happened, you're checking what DIDN'T happen. Without negative verification, you might have a passing test that silently allows unwanted side effects. It's the difference between "email was sent" (positive) and "email was definitely not sent" (negative).

sections.title: Negative Verification Example
Key Points
content: **verify(mock, never())**: asserts a specific method was not called with the given arguments
**verifyNoInteractions(mock)**: stricter — asserts no methods at all were called on the mock
**verifyNoMoreInteractions(mock)**: verifies that after explicit verify() calls, no other methods were invoked
**Negative scenarios**: essential for testing validation failures, permission checks, and conditional branches
**Side effects**: prevents bugs where unwanted actions (like sending email or saving to DB) happen in error paths
**Argument matchers**: use any(), eq() with never() just like with regular verify()
**Multiple verifications**: you can chain multiple never() checks for different methods on the same mock

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: To verify that a method was never called in Mockito, you use verify with the never mode. The syntax is verify, then in parentheses the mock, comma, never with parentheses, dot method name. For example, verify emailService comma never dot sendConfirmation with any Order. This asserts that sendConfirmation was not invoked at all during the test. You'd use this to test negative scenarios — situations where a side effect should NOT happen. Let's say you're testing an order service and the order fails validation because it's missing required fields. You want to verify two things: first, the order was not saved to the database, and second, no confirmation email was sent. So you'd write verify orderRepository comma never dot save with any, and verify emailService comma never dot sendConfirmation with any. This catches a bug where your code might still call these methods even when validation fails. There's also verifyNoInteractions, which is stricter. It asserts that absolutely no methods were called on the mock, not even getter methods. Use that when you want to be sure the mock was completely untouched. One common mistake is only testing the happy path — verifying that methods WERE called — but not testing the error path where they should NOT be called. That leaves bugs undetected. Negative verification is how you test the negative space in your logic.

questions.question: How do you set up Mockito in a Spring Boot project?
questions.title: Mockito Setup in Spring Boot
questions.direct_answer: Spring Boot's spring-boot-starter-test dependency includes Mockito automatically; add @ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class) for pure unit tests.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know how Mockito fits into the Spring Boot test ecosystem without manual configuration
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Manually adding mockito-core when spring-boot-starter-test already provides it, causing version conflicts
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Distinguish between mockito-core, mockito-junit-jupiter, and when each is needed

sections.title: Mockito in Spring Boot Projects
sections.content: **Spring Boot** makes Mockito setup nearly zero-configuration because **spring-boot-starter-test** bundles **mockito-core** and **mockito-junit-jupiter** out of the box. When you add this starter to your `pom.xml` or `build.gradle`, you get Mockito, JUnit 5, AssertJ, and other test libraries in a single dependency. For **pure unit tests** (testing a class without Spring context), add **@ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class)** to your test class and use @Mock/@InjectMocks as usual. For **integration tests** that need Spring context, use **@SpringBootTest** or **@WebMvcTest** which include Mockito support via **@MockBean** for mocking Spring-managed beans. The key insight: you don't manually add Mockito JARs — Spring Boot's opinionated dependency management handles versioning and compatibility. Think of it like ordering a combo meal: you get all the test tools together, pre-configured to work as a set.

sections.title: Mockito in Spring Boot Test
Key Points
content: **spring-boot-starter-test**: includes mockito-core, mockito-junit-jupiter, JUnit 5, AssertJ, Hamcrest in one dependency
**No manual setup**: Spring Boot's dependency management handles Mockito versioning — you don't add mockito-core separately
**@ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class)**: use for pure unit tests without Spring context
**@MockBean**: Spring-specific annotation that creates a mock and registers it in the Spring application context
**Version alignment**: spring-boot-starter-test ensures all test libraries are compatible versions
**mockito-junit-jupiter**: provides JUnit 5 integration — already included, you don't need to add it explicitly
**Gradle/Maven**: add spring-boot-starter-test with test scope — it pulls in all testing dependencies transitively

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: Setting up Mockito in a Spring Boot project is really straightforward because Spring Boot includes it automatically. When you add the spring-boot-starter-test dependency to your pom or build file, you get Mockito core, Mockito JUnit Jupiter integration, JUnit 5, AssertJ, and other test libraries all in one bundle. You don't need to manually add mockito-core or worry about version compatibility — Spring Boot's dependency management handles that for you. For pure unit tests where you're testing a class without loading Spring context, you just add at-ExtendWith MockitoExtension dot class to your test class, then use at-Mock and at-InjectMocks like normal. For integration tests where you need Spring context, you use at-SpringBootTest or at-WebMvcTest, and if you need to mock a Spring-managed bean, you use at-MockBean instead of at-Mock. At-MockBean creates the mock and registers it in the Spring application context, replacing the real bean. One common mistake freshers make is manually adding mockito-core to their dependencies when it's already included via the starter. This can cause version conflicts if the manual version doesn't match what Spring Boot expects. The key insight is that spring-boot-starter-test is your one-stop dependency for all testing tools — it's Spring Boot's opinionated test stack, and it includes Mockito by default.

questions.direct_answer: Mockito.mock(Class.class) creates mocks programmatically, while @Mock is annotation-based and requires MockitoExtension or MockitoAnnotations.openMocks() to initialize.

sections.title: Two Approaches to Creating Mocks
sections.content: **Mockito.mock()** and **@Mock** both create mock objects, but they differ in **how** and **when** the mock is created. The **static method** `Mockito.mock(ClassName.class)` is **imperative**: you call it explicitly in your code, and it returns a mock immediately. You control the timing and lifecycle. The **annotation** `@Mock` is **declarative**: you annotate a field, and **MockitoExtension** (in JUnit 5) or **MockitoAnnotations.openMocks()** scans and initializes it before tests run. Think of it like manual vs. automatic transmission: the static method gives you control, the annotation gives you convenience. The annotation approach is preferred in modern tests because it integrates with JUnit's lifecycle, reduces boilerplate, and automatically enables **strict stubbing** mode to catch test quality issues.

sections.title: When to Use Each Approach
sections.content: **Use @Mock** for standard test class fields when you're writing typical unit tests. It's cleaner, requires less code, and integrates with JUnit 5's lifecycle. The MockitoExtension handles initialization, injection via @InjectMocks, and automatic reset between tests. You also get strict stubbing enabled by default, which improves test quality by catching unused or mismatched stubs. This is the **default choice** for 90% of scenarios. **Use Mockito.mock()** when you need dynamic creation — for example, creating mocks in a loop, conditionally based on test parameters, or in utility methods that build complex test fixtures. It's also useful when working with generic types where annotation syntax is awkward, or when you're writing test code outside a JUnit test class (like in a standalone test helper). The programmatic approach gives you control but sacrifices the automatic lifecycle management and strict stubbing that comes with the annotation style.

sections.title: Key Points
content: **@Mock**: declarative, scanned by MockitoExtension, preferred for standard test fields
**Mockito.mock()**: imperative, called explicitly, useful for dynamic creation and helper methods
**Strict stubbing**: automatically enabled with @Mock via MockitoExtension, manual with static method
**Lifecycle**: @Mock mocks are reset between tests automatically; manual mocks require explicit management
**@ExtendWith**: required for @Mock to work — without it, annotated fields stay null
**@InjectMocks**: only works with @Mock fields — can't inject programmatically created mocks automatically
**Code clarity**: @Mock reduces boilerplate and makes dependencies visible at the field level

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: Mockito dot mock and the at-Mock annotation both create mock objects, but they differ in how and when that happens. The static method Mockito dot mock takes a class and immediately returns a mock instance. You call it explicitly in your test code, like var mock equals Mockito dot mock UserRepository dot class. It works anywhere without any setup — it's just a method call. The at-Mock annotation is declarative. You put it on a field, and then the MockitoExtension scans your test class before each test and creates the mock for you. You don't write any initialization code — it happens automatically. The annotation approach is preferred in modern tests for a few reasons. First, it's cleaner — you declare what you need at the field level, and the framework handles the rest. Second, it integrates with JUnit's lifecycle, so mocks are automatically reset between tests. Third, and this is important, the MockitoExtension enables strict stubbing by default. That means if you stub a method but never call it, or call it with different arguments, Mockito fails the test. That catches bugs that the programmatic approach would miss. You'd use the static method when you need dynamic creation, like creating mocks in a loop or based on test input, or in helper methods that build test fixtures. One common mistake is using at-Mock without the at-ExtendWith annotation. If you forget that, the extension never runs, so your at-Mock fields stay null and your test crashes with NullPointerException. The extension is what activates the annotation processing.

questions.question: What does MockitoSession do and how does it differ from MockitoJUnitRunner?
questions.title: MockitoSession vs MockitoJUnitRunner
questions.direct_answer: MockitoSession is a programmatic, JUnit-agnostic way to initialise mocks and enforce strict stubbing; MockitoJUnitRunner is a JUnit 4-specific runner that does the same automatically.

interviewer_intent.testing: Familiarity with different Mockito initialisation approaches and their trade-offs
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using MockitoJUnitRunner in a JUnit 5 project where it is not supported
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that MockitoSession is preferred in JUnit 5 or framework-agnostic contexts and enforces strictness without requiring a specific runner

sections.title: MockitoSession vs MockitoJUnitRunner
sections.content: **MockitoSession** is a **programmatic API** introduced in Mockito 2 that lets you initialize mocks and enforce strict stubbing manually, independent of any test framework. You create it with `Mockito.mockitoSession()`, start it in a setup method, and finish it in teardown. It's **JUnit-agnostic** — works with JUnit 4, JUnit 5, TestNG, or even no framework. **MockitoJUnitRunner** is a **JUnit 4 runner** that automatically handles mock initialization and strict stubbing by integrating with JUnit 4's runner extension point. You use it with `@RunWith(MockitoJUnitRunner.class)`. Think of MockitoSession as manual gear shifting — you control when initialization happens — while MockitoJUnitRunner is automatic, but locked to JUnit 4. In **JUnit 5**, neither is needed because **@ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class)** is the modern replacement, providing the same functionality with the new extension model.

sections.title: MockitoSession vs MockitoJUnitRunner
Key Points
content: **MockitoSession**: programmatic API for mock initialization, strict stubbing, and lifecycle management — framework-agnostic
**MockitoJUnitRunner**: JUnit 4 runner that automatically handles @Mock/@InjectMocks initialization — JUnit 4 only
**JUnit 5 migration**: MockitoJUnitRunner doesn't work in JUnit 5 — use @ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class) instead
**Strict stubbing**: both enforce strict mode, but MockitoSession requires explicit startMocking()/finishMocking() calls
**Manual control**: MockitoSession gives fine-grained control over when initialization happens — useful in complex setups
**Lifecycle**: MockitoSession must be finished in teardown; runner handles this automatically
**Modern approach**: in JUnit 5, prefer MockitoExtension over both — it's cleaner and idiomatic

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: MockitoSession and MockitoJUnitRunner both handle mock initialization and strict stubbing, but they're designed for different contexts. MockitoJUnitRunner is a JUnit 4 runner — you use it with at-RunWith MockitoJUnitRunner dot class at the top of your test class. It automatically processes at-Mock and at-InjectMocks annotations before each test and enforces strict stubbing. It's convenient but locked to JUnit 4. In JUnit 5, runners don't exist — the extension model replaced them — so MockitoJUnitRunner won't work. MockitoSession is a programmatic API that's framework-agnostic. You create it manually with Mockito dot mockitoSession, call startMocking in a setup method, and finishMocking in teardown. It's more verbose but works with any test framework — JUnit 4, JUnit 5, TestNG, or no framework at all. You'd use it when you need explicit control over mock lifecycle, or when you're not using a framework that has a Mockito extension. One common mistake is trying to use MockitoJUnitRunner in a JUnit 5 project. That won't work because JUnit 5 doesn't support the old runner API. The JUnit 5 equivalent is at-ExtendWith MockitoExtension dot class, which is cleaner and idiomatic. In modern projects, you'd almost never use MockitoSession directly unless you're writing framework-agnostic test utilities. The extension handles everything automatically and integrates with JUnit's lifecycle. MockitoSession is the low-level tool underneath, but the extension is the high-level interface you should use.

questions.question: How do you reset or clear a mock between tests, and when is that necessary?
questions.title: Resetting Mocks Between Tests
questions.direct_answer: Use Mockito.reset(mock) to wipe all stubbings and recorded interactions, but it is usually a design smell — prefer creating fresh mocks per test via @Mock with a proper test lifecycle.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of mock lifecycle and test isolation
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Sharing a single mock instance across all tests in a static field and then resetting it
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that Mockito.reset() is a code smell indicating shared state; the fix is per-test mock creation

sections.title: Resetting Mocks and When It's Necessary
sections.content: **Mockito.reset(mock)** clears all stubbings and recorded interactions from a mock, returning it to a blank state. You'd call it when you need to reuse a mock across multiple tests but want a clean slate. However, this is almost always a **design smell** indicating **shared state** between tests. The root problem: you're reusing the same mock instance across tests, which violates **test isolation**. Each test should be independent — setup in test A shouldn't affect test B. Think of it like washing a coffee mug: if you need to reset it, you're probably sharing it when you should have a clean mug per use. The correct approach is to create **fresh mocks per test** using **@Mock** with **@ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class)** in JUnit 5, which automatically creates new instances before each test. Mockito.reset() is a crutch for bad test design, not a standard practice.

sections.title: Anti-Pattern and Correct Pattern
Key Points
content: **Mockito.reset(mock)**: clears all stubbings, recorded interactions, and verification data from a mock
**Design smell**: needing reset() usually means you're sharing mocks across tests, violating isolation
**Test isolation**: each test should have independent setup — no state from previous tests should leak
**@Mock lifecycle**: with MockitoExtension, @Mock fields are new instances per test automatically
**Static mocks**: the most common cause of needing reset — storing mocks in static fields shared across tests
**Performance myth**: creating new mocks is extremely fast — resetting for performance is premature optimization
**Legitimate use**: the only valid case is integration tests where mock creation is expensive (like database connections), but that's rare

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: You can reset a mock by calling Mockito dot reset and passing the mock instance. This clears all stubbings and recorded interactions, returning the mock to a clean state. But here's the key: if you find yourself needing to reset a mock, that's usually a code smell indicating bad test design. The root problem is shared state — you're reusing the same mock instance across multiple tests. For example, you might have a static field holding a mock, and you reset it in an AfterEach method. That violates test isolation. Each test should be independent. If test A stubs the mock to return a specific value, that stub shouldn't affect test B. The correct fix is to create fresh mocks per test. In JUnit 5, you use at-Mock fields with at-ExtendWith MockitoExtension dot class. The extension creates new mock instances before each test automatically, so every test starts with a clean slate. You don't need to reset anything. One misconception freshers have is thinking that creating new mocks is expensive, so they optimize by reusing and resetting. That's wrong. Creating mocks is extremely fast — Mockito does it thousands of times per second. Resetting is premature optimization that trades test quality for no real benefit. The only legitimate case for reset is in integration tests where the object being mocked is expensive to create, like a database connection pool, but that's rare and you should rethink why you're mocking something that expensive. Bottom line: if you're calling Mockito dot reset, step back and refactor to per-test mock creation instead.
